body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Care bundle compliance and surgical site infection after colorectal resection: a prospective multicentre study","authors":"Achebe-Sandoval R, Lindqvist-Mwangi P, Okonkwo-Hartley J","year":2020,"venue":"Journal of Colorectal Surgical Quality","doi":"10.5555/jcsq.2020.0211","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In 2,140 colorectal resections across 11 hospitals, full compliance with a six-element bundle was recorded in 38 percent. Surgical site infection occurred in 9.8 percent of fully compliant cases and 16.1 percent of others (adjusted odds ratio 0.61, 95 percent CI 0.46 to 0.81). Oral antibiotic bowel preparation and wound protectors showed the strongest individual associations. Infection was ascertained by active surveillance until day 30, including a telephone review after discharge. Compliance was recorded by theatre staff who knew the study aim, and emergency cases were fewer than a fifth of the sample."},{"title":"Which bundle elements matter? An element-level analysis in elective colorectal surgery","authors":"Petrov-Halvorsen M, Nakashima-Obi T","year":2018,"venue":"Surgical Infection Practice","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using data on 860 elective colorectal resections, we examined each of seven bundle elements. Oral antibiotic prophylaxis with bowel preparation was associated with lower infection (odds ratio 0.52), while glove change before closure showed no clear association. Elements were strongly correlated with each other, so individual estimates are unstable and should not be used to drop elements. Emergency cases were excluded, and compliance was taken from the operation note rather than recorded at the time. The authors call for prospective recording of each element at the time of surgery."},{"title":"Surgical site infection bundles in colorectal surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis","authors":"Castellanos-Fairweather L, Oyelowo-Brandt E, Sato-Nilsen K, Reid-Achterberg D","year":2023,"venue":"Surgical Evidence Reviews","doi":"10.5555/ser.2023.0119","providerType":"review","abstract":"Across 24 studies, most of them before-and-after comparisons, bundles were associated with lower surgical site infection after colorectal surgery (risk ratio 0.56, 95 percent CI 0.46 to 0.68). Studies with higher compliance reported larger reductions. Heterogeneity was high and bundle contents varied from 4 to 12 elements. Only 5 studies included post-discharge surveillance, so infections diagnosed after discharge were probably missed in most studies. Bundles that included oral antibiotic preparation reported the largest reductions, and publication bias was likely because small studies without an effect were rarely reported."},{"title":"Post-discharge surveillance and missed surgical site infections after colorectal surgery","authors":"Mensah-Kowalski A, Dubois-Tanaka H","year":2021,"venue":"Infection Surveillance Methods","doi":"10.5555/ism.2021.0087","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Of 412 surgical site infections detected after colorectal resection in three hospitals, 47 percent were diagnosed after discharge. A telephone call at day 30 by a surveillance nurse detected 83 percent of the post-discharge infections found by a combined clinic and telephone approach. Patients who could not be reached by phone were older and more often lived alone. Without post-discharge surveillance, infection rates would have been underestimated by almost half. Infections found after discharge were more often superficial but still led to unplanned clinic visits and readmissions."},{"title":"Defining compliance when bundle elements do not apply: all-or-none measurement with applicability rules","authors":"Ferreira-Oduya S, Holm-Adeyemi C","year":2016,"venue":"Quality Measurement in Surgery","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared ways of scoring full bundle compliance when some elements do not apply. Counting non-applicable elements as delivered inflated full compliance in emergency cases from 31 to 44 percent, while excluding cases with any non-applicable element removed most emergency cases. An all-or-none score over applicable elements, with written applicability rules agreed in advance, gave stable estimates and could be completed in under two minutes on a paper form. Agreement between two independent scorers was high when the applicability rules were written down in advance."},{"title":"Emergency colorectal surgery and surgical site infection: contamination, stoma formation and bundle delivery","authors":"Varga-Nwosu B, Kimura-Lindgren A, Brennan-Mbeki O","year":2024,"venue":"Journal of Colorectal Surgical Quality","doi":"10.5555/jcsq.2024.0048","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In 1,030 emergency colorectal resections, surgical site infection occurred in 21 percent. Faecal contamination (odds ratio 2.4) and stoma formation were the strongest predictors. Full bundle compliance was recorded in only 19 percent of emergency cases, mainly because normothermia and glucose control were not documented. The authors warn that comparing compliant and non-compliant cases without adjusting for emergency status and contamination will exaggerate any bundle effect. Wound protectors were used in only half of emergency cases, and infection rates were similar across surgeons once contamination and stoma formation were taken into account."},{"title":"Normothermia and glucose control during colorectal surgery: measurement from anaesthesia records","authors":"Tanaka-Achebe F, Laurent-Sorensen G","year":2019,"venue":"Anaesthesia Quality Reports","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Reviewing 600 anaesthesia records for colorectal resections, we found an end-of-surgery temperature below 36.0 degrees in 18 percent of patients and no glucose measurement in 41 percent of patients without diabetes. Electronic anaesthesia records captured temperature reliably, but glucose values were often recorded only on paper charts. The authors recommend recording both elements at the end of surgery on the bundle form rather than extracting them later from anaesthesia records. Hypothermia was more common in operations lasting more than three hours and in patients over 80."}]}
